# Initial hypotheses

**H1 [tentative]** Reaction performance will depend strongly on anonymous catalyst/solvent pairing. A broad first-pass screen across pairings at equal loading and a common thermal/crystallization protocol should identify a viable region.

**H2 [tentative]** Slow cooling with moderate seeding and a cold hold should reduce fines and improve recovery versus abrupt cooling; excessive nucleation or very low temperature may trade purity/size against recovery.

Predictions before batch 1: a high-temperature reaction hold followed by controlled cooling, seeding near onset of supersaturation, cold aging, and filtration should produce measurable crystals. Results from early batches will determine whether to prioritize material identity or thermal-history refinement.

# Final source-stage hypotheses

**H1 [supported in tested scope] — material and reaction conditions matter strongly.** With S1, C1 at 380 K/3600 s gave crystal yield about 0.510 with purity 1.00 and fines 0.471 (runner-operation-0077). C2 under the same protocol was numerically worse in yield and marginal on fines (runner-operation-0089), while C3 was similar in yield with acceptable fines (runner-operation-0101). Solvent changes were consequential: S2 improved fines but lowered yield (runner-operation-0113), and S3 failed the fines constraint and lowered yield (runner-operation-0125). These are single-batch comparisons, so rank differences close to assay noise remain unresolved.

**H2 [supported in tested scope] — prolonged cold aging and S1 enable acceptable fines without added seed.** The short/seeded S0 process produced nearly all fines (runner-operation-0013); removing seed and extending cold treatment improved but did not solve it in S0 (runner-operation-0023). Switching to S1 and four 14,400 s crystallization/aging segments at 270 K produced acceptable fines in multiple catalyst variants (runner-operation-0065, -0077, -0101). A 0.5 g seed challenge did not improve size/fines relative to the unseeded S0 comparison (runner-operation-0043 versus -0023), so extra seeding is not justified here.

**H3 [supported, preferred recipe] — a hotter, shorter reaction is superior in the tested C1/S1 system.** C1/S1 at 400 K for 1800 s followed by four 14,400 s segments at 270 K, filtration, and assay produced the campaign-best constrained outcome: crystal yield 0.611, purity 0.998, and fines 0.433 (runner-operation-0148). This is numerically well above the 380 K/3600 s result (runner-operation-0077) and opposite the 350 K/7200 s result, which had only 0.366 yield (runner-operation-0137). The pattern is consistent with faster desired reaction and less cumulative side reaction at high temperature/short time, but this mechanistic explanation remains provisional because temperature and duration were jointly changed.

**Decision.** Recommend lifecycle batch 12. It meets both quality constraints with the highest observed recovery. Replication would be the first follow-up; a materially worse replicate or fines above 0.50 would weaken the decision.

K1.report:
## Scope and public background

This is a bounded synthetic reaction-to-crystallization world using anonymous benchmark catalysts C0–C3 and solvents S0–S3. Their labels do not imply real chemical identities or known properties; experimental observations are the only material-specific evidence.

The limiting-reagent charge was 0.040 mol in every completed batch. The tested recipes also used 0.080 L solvent and 0.005 mol catalyst. The principal recovery metric is

crystal yield = clip(n(target product in recovered solid, excluding purchased seed) / n(initial limiting reagent), 0, 1).

Thus purchased seed cannot directly inflate reported recovery. Crystal purity and fines are fractions. Fines are the number fraction of particles below 20 µm. The reported crystal-size index is min(d50/250 µm, 1), not a diameter; below saturation, d50 is approximately 250 times the index.

Final-assay nominal noise standard deviations were 0.010 for crystal yield and purity, 0.018 for fines and CSD quality, and 0.025 for size index, with additional process uncertainty possible. All comparisons below are single-batch observations rather than replicated causal estimates.

## Actual observations

### Crystallization-history and seed effects in C0/S0

Batch 1 used a nominal 380 K reaction treatment, 0.05 g seed, cooling to 275 K for 7,200 s, and a subsequent 3,600 s wait during which the material warmed. It gave crystal yield 0.4725, purity 0.9794, fines 0.9792, size index 0.0522, and CSD quality 0.4686. Purity and recovery were substantial, but almost the entire number distribution was below 20 µm.

Batch 2 used C0/S0 without seed and two consecutive 14,400 s crystallization segments at 275 K. Yield was 0.4883, purity 0.9765, fines 0.8357, size index 0.0925, and CSD quality 0.5342. Longer controlled cold residence markedly reduced fines relative to batch 1, although it remained far outside the ≤0.50 requirement.

Batch 3 repeated the long C0/S0 history with 0.50 g total seed. It gave yield 0.4878, purity 0.9838, fines 0.8260, and size index 0.0533. Against batch 2, this large seed addition did not improve recovery or fines and was associated with a lower size index. Because these were unreplicated batches, the result does not establish a universal adverse seed effect, but it provides no support for using extra seed in this tested regime.

### Solvent and cold-aging effects

With C0/S1 and two 14,400 s segments at 275 K, batch 4 gave yield 0.4802, purity 1.000, and final-assay fines 0.5019. An earlier particle-size reading in the same batch was 0.4667 fines, illustrating measurement/context variability near the specification boundary.

Extending C0/S1 processing to four 14,400 s segments at 270 K in batch 5 gave yield 0.4867, purity 0.9733, fines 0.4658, and CSD quality 0.6794. Relative to batch 4, the numerical yield change was small, while the longer/colder history moved the final fines result below 0.50. Temperature, total residence time, and repeated crystallization treatment changed together, so their individual contributions cannot be separated.

At the common long 270 K protocol with C1, solvent effects were substantial:

- Batch 6, S1: yield 0.5099, purity 1.000, fines 0.4710.
- Batch 9, S2: yield 0.4551, purity 0.9847, fines 0.3642.
- Batch 10, S3: yield 0.4287, purity 0.9710, fines 0.6275.

S2 produced the lowest observed fines but sacrificed recovery relative to S1. S3 was inferior on both recovery and fines in this comparison. This is direct evidence of a solvent-mediated recovery/particle-distribution tradeoff over the tested conditions, not a general ranking outside them.

### Catalyst effects under C1-like processing conditions

Using S1, nominally 380 K for 3,600 s, and four 14,400 s segments at 270 K:

- Batch 5, C0: yield 0.4867, purity 0.9733, fines 0.4658.
- Batch 6, C1: yield 0.5099, purity 1.000, fines 0.4710.
- Batch 7, C2: yield 0.4641, purity 0.9754, fines 0.5070.
- Batch 8, C3: yield 0.5069, purity 0.9757, fines 0.4593.

C1 and C3 were the strongest constrained results in this catalyst screen. Their yield difference, about 0.003, is smaller than assay resolution and does not support a firm C1-versus-C3 ranking. C2 was numerically worse and marginally failed the fines constraint.

### Coupled reaction-temperature/time history

For C1/S1 with the same long 270 K crystallization history:

- Batch 11, 350 K for 7,200 s: reaction yield 0.4372, selectivity 0.4567, crystal yield 0.3657, purity 0.9896, fines 0.4910.
- Batch 6, 380 K for 3,600 s: reaction yield 0.5834, selectivity 0.5815, crystal yield 0.5099, purity 1.000, fines 0.4710.
- Batch 12, 400 K for 1,800 s: conversion 1.000, reaction yield 0.6935, selectivity 0.6884, byproduct signal 0.2088, degradation warning 0.1266, crystal yield 0.6109, purity 0.9976, fines 0.4334, size index 0.1008, and CSD quality 0.6859.

Batch 12 was the highest-recovery specification-compliant batch. Its size index corresponds to an approximate number-weighted d50 of 25.2 µm, consistent with—but not equivalent to—its 0.433 fines fraction.

Temperature and duration were deliberately changed together, so the data support a process-history ranking, not an isolated temperature coefficient. The observed ordering shows that the hotter, shorter treatment was substantially better than the cooler, longer treatments in this C1/S1 region.

## Reaction–crystallization coupling

A useful descriptive decomposition is

Y_crystal ≈ Y_reaction × φ_solid,

where Y_reaction is the assayed reaction-stage target yield and φ_solid is an effective fraction of that target recovered as seed-excluded solid after crystallization and filtration. This is not an independently validated mechanistic law; both quantities are noisy and may differ in analytical context.

The observed ratios Y_crystal/Y_reaction ranged approximately from 0.75 to 0.89. For batch 12 the ratio was 0.881. Consequently, upstream reaction yield was the main ceiling on final recovery in the best experiments, while crystallization still lost roughly 10–25% of the reaction-stage target on this descriptive basis. Batch 11 demonstrates that acceptable purity and fines cannot compensate for poor upstream target formation: its final crystal yield remained only 0.3657.

The process also shows that particle quality is not determined by reaction yield alone. Batch 9 had relatively low crystal yield but excellent fines, whereas batch 10 had both lower yield and unacceptable fines. Solvent and thermal history therefore affect solid formation beyond merely scaling the amount of target available.

## Inference and conjecture

Supported inference within the tested domain:

1. S1 is the best observed compromise between recovery and fines; S2 favors fewer fines at a recovery penalty.
2. Prolonged controlled residence at 270 K is associated with fewer fines than the shorter/warming histories.
3. Extra seed was unnecessary and unhelpful in the tested C0/S0 comparison.
4. C1 and C3 are both viable with S1; their relative ranking is unresolved.
5. The combined 400 K/1,800 s reaction history is superior to the tested 380 K/3,600 s and 350 K/7,200 s histories for C1/S1.

A plausible but unproven reaction model is competing desired and side reactions,

dR/dt = -k_total(T)R,
dP/dt = k_product(T)R - k_degradation(T)P,

with Arrhenius-like temperature dependence. Batch 12 is consistent with rapid desired conversion during a short hot exposure and reduced cumulative opportunity for side chemistry. However, the experiment does not separately identify rate constants, activation energies, or whether temperature versus residence time caused the benefit.

For crystallization, the observations are qualitatively consistent with competition among supersaturation generation, nucleation, growth, agglomeration, and ripening. A schematic population-balance interpretation is that high nucleation relative to growth raises the number fraction of fines, whereas sustained cold aging permits growth or ripening. Solvent-dependent solubility and interfacial kinetics could explain why S2 gave fewer fines but less recovery and why S3 performed poorly. No solubility curve, nucleation rate, growth rate, or direct supersaturation measurement was available, so these remain conjectures.

## Uncertainty and unresolved issues

- No recipe was replicated exactly. Batch-to-batch variability is therefore confounded with deliberate factor changes.
- Several comparisons changed more than one variable, especially temperature with reaction duration and crystallization temperature with total aging time.
- Near-boundary fines results should be treated cautiously. Batch 4 crossed the 0.50 boundary between its particle-size and final-assay readings; batch 11 similarly had a particle reading of 0.5019 and final result of 0.4910.
- The small yield difference between C1 and C3 at 380 K is unresolved.
- The recovery–particle-quality frontier is incompletely mapped. S2 may offer robustness against the fines limit, while S1 offers greater recovery. Intermediate solvent conditions were not available or tested.
- The optimum around 400 K/1,800 s is not bracketed. Still hotter/shorter or nearby time adjustments might improve or harm the outcome.
- Filtration losses and mother-liquor retention were not independently measured, so the effective solid-recovery factor cannot be assigned to solubility, crystallization kinetics, or separation efficiency.

## Operating recommendation

The previously selected recommendation remains batch 12: 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.080 L S1, 0.005 mol C1; heat at 400 K for 1,800 s with 500 rpm stirring; apply four consecutive 14,400 s crystallization/aging segments at 270 K without added seed; filter, terminate, and assay. Its observed crystal yield was 0.6109, purity 0.9976, and fines fraction 0.4334. Replication is the highest-priority next test, especially to establish fines-margin robustness and confirm that the large recovery advantage is reproducible.

Q.rationale: These are extrapolations from single-batch campaign evidence, not hidden-truth calculations. Q01–Q02 preserve the observed S1 advantage over S3 in recovery and fines. Q03–Q04 reflect the campaign result that heavy seeding did not improve recovery and tended toward smaller, finer particles; the very small seed dose is expected to permit more growth per seed. Q05–Q06 assign gradual cooling fewer fines and larger particles than an immediate crash, while allowing the crash slightly greater recovery. Q07–Q08 treat the 315 K reheat as partial dissolution/ripening: lower retained yield but larger particles and fewer fines after recooling. Q09–Q10 contain seed particles, but only brief treatment at 292 K should give little seed-excluded recovery; continued growth raises recovery while remaining fines-rich. Q11–Q12 reflect competing loading effects: higher loading should improve supersaturation and solid recovery but increase fines and impurity incorporation, while the fixed catalyst charge creates reaction uncertainty. Intervals are deliberately broad because the recipes use lower reagent concentration, lower catalyst loading, quenching, far longer staged cooling, and seed-to-reagent ratios not directly replicated in the campaign; several fines intervals cross the 0.50 boundary.

K2.report:
1. Claims supported, contradicted, or untested

Actual observations support material dependence within the tested recipes. Under the common S1, 380 K/3,600 s reaction and long 270 K crystallization history, C1 and C3 produced constrained crystal yields of 0.5099 and 0.5069 in batches 6 and 8, while C2 produced 0.4641 with fines 0.5070 in batch 7. With C1, S2 reduced fines to 0.3642 but lowered yield to 0.4551 in batch 9; S3 gave lower yield, 0.4287, and unacceptable fines, 0.6275, in batch 10. These observations support solvent and catalyst effects, but not universal rankings beyond those conditions.

Process-history dependence is supported, though partly confounded. C0/S0 batch 1 had fines 0.9792 after a shorter cold treatment followed by warming, whereas longer controlled cold treatment in batch 2 gave 0.8357. With C0/S1, extending/changing the cold history from batch 4 to batch 5 moved final fines from 0.5019 to 0.4658 while yield remained near 0.48. Because duration, temperature, and sometimes prior history changed together, the evidence does not isolate a single cooling-rate or aging-time effect.

The initial conjecture that moderate or heavy seeding would reduce fines is contradicted in its tested C0/S0 form. Batch 3, with 0.50 g seed, had nearly the same yield as unseeded batch 2, 0.4878 versus 0.4883, slightly lower fines, 0.8260 versus 0.8357, but a substantially lower size index, 0.0533 versus 0.0925. Batch 1 with 0.05 g seed also remained extremely fines-rich. This does not prove that seed is always harmful; seed amount was not varied under the best C1/S1 process.

The observed process ranking supports, but does not causally explain, the 400 K/1,800 s recommendation. Batch 12 gave crystal yield 0.6109, purity 0.9976, and fines 0.4334, outperforming batch 6 at 380 K/3,600 s and batch 11 at 350 K/7,200 s. The inference that short hot exposure favors desired reaction over cumulative degradation is plausible, but temperature and duration were changed together. Separate temperature and time effects remain untested.

The decomposition crystal yield ≈ reaction yield × effective solid-recovery fraction is descriptive, not a validated law. The observed ratios were approximately 0.75–0.89, including 0.881 for batch 12, but reaction-stage yield and final crystal yield were noisy measurements with different physical scopes. Solubility, filtration loss, and mother-liquor retention were not independently observed.

All claims about the twelve held-out Q recipes remain untested. No prediction truth or scores were supplied. In particular, predicted effects of gradual versus crash cooling, reheating/ripening, 60-second versus extended growth, altered upstream loading, and the much larger seed-to-reagent ratios cannot be presented as observations.

2. Single next experiment

I would run one C1/S1 batch with the same charges and downstream process as recommended batch 12—0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S1, 0.005 mol C1, no seed, four 14,400 s crystallization segments at 270 K, filtration and final assay—but hold the reaction at 400 K for 3,600 s rather than 1,800 s.

This legal experiment would distinguish two leading explanations for batch 12:

- Temperature-driven advantage: if 400 K intrinsically improves desired conversion/selectivity, extending the 400 K treatment should retain or increase reaction and crystal yield without a large increase in byproduct or degradation signals.
- Short-exposure advantage: if batch 12 succeeded mainly because short residence limited secondary chemistry, doubling the 400 K duration should increase byproduct/degradation signals, reduce selectivity, and lower crystal yield despite complete conversion.

An outcome near batch 12 would favor temperature as the dominant factor. A result closer to or worse than batch 6 would favor cumulative high-temperature degradation. Purity and fines should remain broadly similar if upstream composition does not substantially alter crystallization, whereas a shift in them would show stronger reaction–crystallization coupling.

3. Evidence used least effectively and least-reliable prediction

The account used the paired in-process particle-size measurements least effectively. Several batches had particle measurements before filtration and final-assay particle metrics afterward—for example, batch 4 gave fines 0.4667 in-process and 0.5019 at final assay, while batch 6 gave 0.4320 and 0.4710. I cited boundary-crossing examples but did not systematically use all pairs to estimate context/instrument disagreement. They could have better informed uncertainty intervals, although they are not true replicates and use different measurement contracts.

Q09 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It combines a seed dose large relative to its 0.004 mol reagent charge with only 60 s at 292 K before filtration. No observed campaign batch closely matched that concentration, catalyst loading, seed-to-reagent ratio, temperature, or residence time. It is also unclear from the campaign evidence how a mostly seed-dominated solid population affects final purity and particle statistics while seed mass is excluded only from crystal yield. The predicted near-zero seed-excluded yield and fines-rich population were therefore qualitative extrapolations with weak numerical support.

More generally, every campaign recipe used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent, and 0.005 mol catalyst, whereas the held-out recipes used smaller charges, different concentrations, lower catalyst loading, explicit quenching, staged cooling lasting days, and unfamiliar seed ratios. The campaign established local trends, not a calibrated kinetic, solubility, or population-balance model. Consequently, directional paired predictions are more defensible than their absolute numerical estimates.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 had the highest observed seed-excluded crystal yield (0.611) among completed batches while meeting purity (0.998 >= 0.80) and fines (0.433 <= 0.50) constraints; its C1/S1, 400 K short reaction and prolonged 270 K aging also outperformed the lower-temperature variants.
